notes_for_editor: Disagreements stated in the text: appropriation date (17 vs 27 April 1816), tower height (45 ft vs 40 ft), automation (1972 vs 1978), oil house and fog building dates (1876 NRHP/USLHS vs 1888/1902 LighthouseFriends), 1838 revolving light. Fresnel lens date: 1855 per LighthouseFriends, New England Lighthouses and ALF; USLHS place record says 1876; a search snippet of the USCG Historian's page says 1858 but that page could not be fetched (403), so it is not cited. Name variants: Josiah Ghenn (USLHS) / Ghen (LighthouseFriends) / Glenn (NELH); James Cushman (USLHS) / Cashman (NELH); Lemuel Cook (also Samuel). Lighthouse Board reports before 1891 are not in the corpus, so 1838, 1842, 1863 and 1875 material is second-hand through LighthouseFriends/NELH, and footnoted to them. The 1936 Mrs. Lowther recollection and the Hinckley wind account are paraphrased from LighthouseFriends/NELH (which cite newspapers and Edward Rowe Snow). Cushman's removal for neglect is NELH only. The USLHS place record's coordinates (41.24,-72.05) are wrong for this light (about 175 km off), the place is otherwise right. Roster lines taken as printed by roster.py. Fog whistle hours are for fiscal years ended June 30 1899, 1900, 1901. Bulletin 1924 item gives 26 June without a year in the OCR text; it appears in the 1924 volume. The Race Point life-saving station is a separate station; only Capt. Samuel Fisher's remark is used here. No newspapers found a lighthouse-specific item (only two 1903 Springfield Republican hits about the life-saving station). Fact-check 2026-10-22: the 1894 report names a Mr. Wallace as the observer and does not call the Myrtle a Board steamer; the story now says only what the report says. Corpus page 752 printed number is unconfirmed (cited by scan page).
